title: Indices post longest losing streak in more than 6 months amid crude worries
text:
The country’s shares ended lower, and benchmark indices posted their longest losing streak in more than six months as the escalating West Asia conflict kept Brent crude prices elevated.

The benchmark Sensex, after declining as much as 1.2 per cent, recovered its losses on Friday and ended the session at 76,060, down 332 points or 0.4 per cent. Nifty, meanwhile, closed at 23,768, a decline of 102 points or 0.4 per cent.

The recovery was aided by a fall in crude prices after three days of gains following disruptions in supplies through the Red Sea.

Both indices posted their fifth consecutive decline. Last time both the indices declined for five continuous sessions from January 5, 2026, to January 9, 2026.

The Sensex declined 2.7 per cent and the Nifty 2.3 per cent this week, their biggest weekly falls since March 13, 2026.

The total market capitalisation (mcap) of BSE-listed firms stood at ₹476 trillion on Friday, a decline of ₹1 trillion from a day earlier. For the week ending July 24, the mcap fell by ₹5.2 trillion.

Brent crude declined 2.6 per cent to $91.4 per barrel. From the recent lows, Brent crude has risen 20 per cent to the current levels.

India is vulnerable to sustained increases in crude prices because it imports most of its oil requirements.

Higher energy costs could increase inflation, widen the trade deficit, weaken the rupee and squeeze profit margins across industries.

Risk appetite remained subdued after markets were rattled this week by an escalating war in West Asia.

Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) were net sellers worth ₹3,893 crore on Friday, while domestic institutions were net buyers worth ₹5,454 crore.

Market breadth was weak, with 2,185 stocks declining and 1,999 advancing.

“Inflationary fears intensified as escalation of the West Asia conflict kept crude oil prices elevated. For domestic investors, concerns were further exacerbated by the return of US tariff-related uncertainties, which have cast a shadow over the outlook for export-oriented sectors,” said Vinod Nair, head of research at Geojit Investments.

Oil retreats below $100

Oil futures prices fell over 3 per cent on Friday but are set for hefty weekly gains because of worsening disruption ⁠to energy flows in the Red Sea and fears of further escalation in the West Asia war.

Brent futures fell $3.59, or 3.57 per cent, to $97.1 a barrel, having settled above $100 in the previous session for the first time since May after Iran-aligned Houthis said they struck two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea. WTI futures were down $3.14, or 3.41 per cent, at $89.05 a barrel, on track for a nearly 8 per cent weekly rise.

“Tensions in the Middle East from the continued US attacks on Iran, additional Houthi involvement and CPC outages have inevitably driven prices up as supply becomes squeezed once again,” said Rystad analyst Janiv Shah.

At the Bab el-Mandeb strait, commodity vessel transits totalled 32 on July 23, up from 26 the day before, according to Kpler data . “In the right seas, ships are still moving... so it’s not a complete blockade as some might have feared,” said Giovanni Staunovo, a UBS analyst.

JPMorgan analysts said that each additional month of disruption to oil supply would add around $7-$8 a barrel to Brent, lifting monthly average prices to around $114 a barrel if disruptions extend to three more months.

[Reuters]
